Across ages 3–35, fewer than 3 in 100 cite distance as the reason for leaving, so the fix is money and time, not blanket primary-school construction. The exception is Class 11–12, where the Ministry reports that school supply has not kept pace.

A note on the brief’s numbers. 68.5% and 8.2% cover Classes 9–12 counted together. Counted separately, Classes 9–10 are 78.7% and 11–12 are 58.4%; the old Class 9–10 dropout measure is 11.5%. We use the separate figures, on which the problem looks bigger, not smaller.

Sources: UDISE+ 2024-25 (Tables 6.1, 6.4, 6.6, 6.13–6.15); AISHE 2023-24; UNDP Human Development Report 2025; UNESCO Institute for Statistics; NSS 75th round (2017-18, ages 3–35, main reason for leaving); ASER 2024. *Post-school study is a college-equivalent participation rate (AISHE college-enrolment basis); each point adds an estimated 0.057 years; team calculation.

India’s score against a moving target

Said plainly. The steady path lands just inside the projected top 75. Only the faster path reaches the top-50 line, with nothing to spare, so read it as top-50 territory, not a guaranteed rank.
